analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal registration and the transfer tax on machine guns, silencers, and short-barreled firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the National Firearms Act drew one cosponsor, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would erase Chapter 53 of the tax code, which contains the National Firearms Act. That 1934 law requires buyers of machine guns, silencers, and short-barreled shotguns and rifles to register the weapon with the federal government and pay a $200 transfer tax. Repealing it would end both the registration requirement and the tax for those weapons.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of silencers, short-barreled rifles and shotguns, and machine guns would save the $200 transfer tax and avoid federal registration and the paperwork that goes with it. Manufacturers and dealers of those items would gain a larger, cheaper market with fewer restrictions on sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Firearm makers, dealers, and accessory buyers

how_it_helps.text: Repealing Chapter 53 of the Internal Revenue Code would eliminate the $200 transfer tax and the federal registration requirement that currently apply to machine guns, silencers, and short-barreled firearms [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the safety consequences of removing the national registry for some of the most dangerous weapons, and the government would lose the tax revenue, though the revenue involved is small.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through lost regulation and oversight

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate the federal registration system for machine guns, silencers, and short-barreled firearms, ending the records and transfer vetting that law enforcement can use to trace those weapons [S2][S3].
It would repeal a tax that has applied to transfers of these weapons since 1934, removing a financial and procedural barrier that currently limits how easily they change hands [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to buyers is a $200 tax saved and less paperwork. The cost is the loss of a national registry covering weapons chosen for special regulation in 1934 precisely because they were seen as unusually dangerous. The scale is lopsided: a modest convenience and price cut for a narrow group of buyers, weighed against removing oversight of the most heavily restricted class of firearms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Madison Cawthorn introduced the bill on July 15, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The bill received one cosponsor, a Republican [S4].
No further action was taken; the Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the National Firearms Act's registration and transfer tax remained in place, so the status quo of federal oversight over machine guns, silencers, and short-barreled firearms was preserved. Firearm manufacturers and sellers of those items lost the chance at a deregulated market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing federal gun registry survived

for.name: Rep. Madison Cawthorn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the National Firearms Act on July 15, 2022.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Internal Revenue Code
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The only support came from a Republican sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor; no Democrat signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: Repeal would remove the $200 transfer tax and registration for silencers, short-barreled firearms, and machine guns, expanding the market for makers and sellers of these items. The gain comes from stripping away a regulatory and revenue system that documents transfers of the most restricted class of weapons, a cost borne by the public in reduced oversight.
